title: Predicting nighttime atmospheric lifetimes of fluorinated VOCs: temperature-dependent NO 3  kinetics for improved climate impact assessments
content: Quantifying the atmospheric persistence and global warming potential of hydrofluorocarbon substitutes under the Kigali Amendment requires accurate temperature-dependent rate constants for both daytime (OH) and nighttime (NO3) degradation pathways. While NO3 radical oxidation represents a major nocturnal sink, experimental temperature-dependent kinetic data and Arrhenius parameters for hydrogen-abstraction reactions with fluorinated volatile organic compounds remain entirely absent due to severe experimental challenges. In this work, we extend and benchmark the multiconformer transition state theory coupled with constrained transition state randomization protocol to predict nighttime NO3 reaction kinetics. The protocol is validated against recommended room-temperature rate constants for 1,1,1-trifluoro-2-methoxyethane (CH3OCH2CF3) and 2,2-difluoroacetaldehyde (CHF2CHO), yielding theoretical values of 1.6 × 10−18 and 8.2 × 10−17 cm3 molecule−1 s−1, respectively, in excellent agreement with experimental data (within factors of 3.2 and 1.4). Comparison with lowest-conformer TST highlights the necessity of multiconformer sampling. Application to fluorotelomer aldehydes (CxF2x+1CH2CHO, x = 1 − 3) reveals tropospheric nocturnal lifetimes at 272 K ranging from 5.1 to 7.0 years. Non-parallel Arrhenius behavior is observed across the series in the 230–320 K range. An exact statistical mechanical decomposition demonstrates that ground-state reactant conformational buffering (∼80%) dominates over barrier lowering (∼19%) in governing this temperature dependence. This benchmarked protocol delivers a cost-effective, high-throughput computational tool to quantify nocturnal lifetimes, refining and advancing comprehensive atmospheric lifetime and climate impact assessments.
